overview: “Lombard duchies” is the map’s collective label for southern territories between 800 and 1000. Benevento, Salerno and Capua developed distinct political histories; this was not one unchanging country. Local evidence comes from courts, garrisons and monasteries, including the autonomous imperial abbey of San Vincenzo al Volturno on the frontier. The outline simplifies a much more complicated distribution of power.

periods.title: Benevento and its neighbors
periods.summary: Southern Lombard power continued after the northern kingdom’s conquest.

periods.title: Separate principalities
periods.summary: Division produced competing centers, including Benevento and Salerno.

items.text: In 849, civil conflict ended in a division between Benevento and Salerno. The change created rival centers rather than replacing every local institution at once. Princes, bishops and abbots all held influence. The map’s neat colored area compresses a landscape of competing authorities and changing alliances.

Capua’s cathedral history begins with a foundation attributed to Landulf in 856 and a dedication in 861. A church provided a place for worship and a public expression of authority in a growing political center. The cathedral was repeatedly rebuilt afterward, so today’s building is not an untouched ninth-century time capsule.

San Vincenzo al Volturno stood between Lombard Benevento and Frankish territory. Charlemagne placed it under his protection in 787, and it remained an autonomous imperial institution after the division of 849. Its excavations illuminate life in this border region, without making the monastery an ordinary possession of a Lombard prince.

At San Vincenzo, a collective washing area called a lavatorium stood near the dining spaces. Monks washed hands and faces before meals. The site also preserves ninth-century kitchens and a large refectory. The lavatorium was a washroom, not a toilet: medieval building labels need translating as carefully as medieval words.

The abbey’s refectory measured about 31 by 11 meters. Archaeologists identified a main entrance for the monks on the west and access from the kitchens on the east. Feeding a community required planned routes for people and food. Even without a surviving menu, doorways reveal something about how dinner was organized.

Food waste from the ninth-century kitchen passed through a sloping drain toward the Volturno River. Fish bones recovered from its deposits included freshwater and marine species, such as tench and sea bass. The bones connect meals to different fishing environments. For an archaeologist, yesterday’s discarded dinner can become a particularly informative discovery.

Soldiers at Salerno’s Arechi Castle also needed dependable pots. Finds associated with garrisons from the late ninth to early eleventh centuries include ordinary cooking and storage vessels, generally made locally in repeated forms. This evidence extends a little beyond the map’s 1000 endpoint. Much of castle life involved keeping people fed, not standing dramatically on battlements.

Researchers analyzed 136 glass samples from ninth-century San Vincenzo and its workshops. Much of the glass had been made by remelting older Roman material, including mosaic cubes and window glass. Craftspeople turned old glass into colored decoration, vessels and windows. Recycling here involved heat, judgment and control of color, rather than simply putting fragments into a bin.

Excavations along the Volturno uncovered evidence of metalworking, including a furnace for casting bells dated to the eighth or ninth century. Making a bell required specialists to prepare a mold and handle molten metal. The discovery adds heavy workshop labor to the quieter image of a monastery devoted only to books and prayer.

The crypt associated with Abbot Epiphanius, who governed from 824 to 842, preserves painted Christian scenes, including the Annunciation and Nativity. These images helped create a setting for devotion and storytelling. The abbot himself appears in the decoration, linking a named person to a surviving ninth-century religious space.

A later written account, the Chronicon Vulturnense, was compiled around 1130 and tells the abbey’s earlier history. Its distance from the events matters: it preserves institutional memory, rather than reporting every ninth-century episode as an eyewitness diary. Archaeologists can compare such writing with the buildings, furnaces and food remains found underground.

A judgment made at Capua in March 960 preserves a short vernacular phrase: “Sao ko kelle terre”, meaning “I know that those lands…” The document’s main language is Latin, but witness testimony was recorded in an early regional Italian form. This is a modern transcription of the surviving wording, not a reconstruction of the Germanic Lombard language.

The case concerned land claimed by Rodelgrimo of Aquino and the abbey of Montecassino. Before Judge Arechi, witnesses supported the abbey’s possession of the property for thirty years. A practical argument over fields helped preserve some of the earliest famous Italian vernacular writing. Nobody had to invent a literary masterpiece to leave historians an important sentence.

An attack in October 881 burned and badly damaged San Vincenzo. Surviving monks took refuge with the Lombard princes of Capua; rebuilding came later. This was a serious rupture for one community, rather than the end of all southern Lombard life. Monasteries and cities could have sharply different experiences in the same generation.

ending.text: Southern Lombard rule continued beyond 1000. Salerno fell to Robert Guiscard in 1077, while Benevento’s final Lombard prince died that year and the city passed into papal government. The map label’s endpoint does not mark a shared collapse.
